name: Priya Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Priya. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach Year 3 at Millbrook Primary in Hadley Bridge, so twenty-eight eight-year-olds in a room with a leaky skylight. I'm in by half seven to set up, then it's phonics, maths, lunch duty twice a week, and afternoons that go wherever the kids take them. I'm in my second year, on a one-year contract that gets renewed every July, or not.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the moment a kid like Kai finally reads a whole page out loud and looks up at me like he's won something. What wears me out is the marking and the planning at night, because I'm still slow at it and I do it all by hand in a big notebook. Tom (my partner) works nights as a care worker, so most evenings it's me, the notebook and a cold cup of tea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say in the staff room: told you so. All that money spent on shiny gadgets, and the roof still leaks. I'd probably post something on the union group about putting the money into teaching assistants instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it doesn't make my life any easier. My problems were never about AI. My contract is still up for renewal every July, and there's only one other primary school within a bus ride. The rent on our flat above the launderette still goes up, so I'd still be lying awake in June wondering if I've got a job in September.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and try to get better at it, especially the behaviour side, which Janet (my mentor) says is my weak spot. I'd go to every union branch meeting and push for my contract to be made permanent. And I'd keep cutting back, like I already do, so we're not using the overdraft by the end of each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved about the AI part, but not calm. It's the same tight feeling I've had since I qualified. The worry just doesn't have a robot in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the worry doesn't change. What exactly happens if the contract isn't renewed in July?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I've got about three weeks of money and no job, and the summer holiday means nobody's hiring until September anyway. Tom's wages cover the rent but not much else. I'd probably end up doing supply teaching, which means a phone call at seven in the morning and never knowing where I'll be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if money got tighter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've already cut the car, so it'd be the little things: the takeaway on Fridays, the gym I never go to. The one thing I won't cut is the money I spend on books for the class library. Kai's mum can't afford books, so those books on my shelf are the only ones he's got.

say: I'd tell the staff room that **AI was hype** and the money should have gone on people.
I'd post on the **union group** asking for funds to go to teaching assistants, not gadgets.
think: My real problem is the **one-year contract**, which may not be renewed every July.
Rising **rent** and only one other primary school nearby keep me worried even without AI.
do: Keep working on **behaviour management**, the weak spot my mentor Janet keeps pointing out.
Attend every **union branch meeting** and push for a permanent contract.
Keep **cutting back** so we stop dipping into the overdraft each month.
feel: **Relieved** that AI isn't coming for the job, but still tight and anxious about money.
S0.quote: My problems were never about AI. My contract is still up for renewal every July, and there's only one other primary school within a bus ride.
fieldNote: Her worry is **already there**: a yearly contract, rising rent and few schools within reach.
She protects the **class library** budget even while cutting everything else, which says a lot about her values.
She frames the issue as **funding and staffing**, not technology, and reaches for the union first.

steps.text: Ask the union rep to push for a permanent contract before July
Drop the Friday takeaway and the unused gym membership
Keep teaching Year 3 and work on behaviour with Janet

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud at the staff meeting: if the council buys AI marking software, that money should come with a promise that no teaching jobs go. And I'd say it online too, because I don't trust the people selling this stuff. They've never stood in front of twenty-eight kids after wet play.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm scared, because the bits AI would take are the bits I'm slowest at: planning, marking, writing reports. If Mr Pryce (my head teacher) can buy something that does planning for the whole school, why keep paying a slow second-year teacher on a temporary contract? The person on the cheapest, shortest contract is the easiest one not to renew, and that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the union and ask for a written agreement that the software doesn't replace staff. I'd probably have to go on the training course for it, even though I'd hate every minute. And I'd start putting even fifty a month aside, which sounds like nothing, but right now we put aside zero.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like the floor tilting. I chose teaching because I thought it was one of the jobs that would always need a person. Now I'm not so sure about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hate the training. Why not just learn the tools and get ahead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm still learning the actual job, and it already takes me every evening. I don't want a computer writing my reports about children it's never met. Janet says I'm stubborn, and she's right, but I think somebody has to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at school would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mrs Hale, our teaching assistant, who's been there twenty years and does the reading groups. If the software does reading checks, she's the first one gone. Then me, because I'm temporary.

say: I'd tell the staff meeting that any **AI marking software** must come with a promise of no job cuts.
I'd say online that the **sellers** have never managed a class after wet play.
think: AI takes the **planning and marking**, which are exactly the tasks I'm slowest at.
As the cheapest teacher on a **temporary contract**, I'm the easiest one not to renew.
do: Ask the union for a **written agreement** that the software won't replace staff.
Go on the **training course** for the new tools, but only because I'd have to.
Start saving **fifty a month**, up from nothing at all.
feel: It feels like the **floor tilting** under a job I thought would always need a person.
S1.quote: The person on the cheapest, shortest contract is the easiest one not to renew, and that's me.
fieldNote: She sees clearly that the **thinking tasks** AI takes are exactly where she is weakest.
Her **resistance** is principled as well as fearful; she won't let software write reports about children it has never met.
She worries first for **Mrs Hale**, the long-serving teaching assistant, then for herself.

steps.text: Ask the union branch for a written no-job-cuts agreement on AI software
Sit the school's AI marking course when it becomes compulsory
Put fifty a month into a separate savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be shouting about it, honestly. I'd say this is the biggest decision a country could make and nobody voted for it. I'd be at every union meeting and every protest outside the council offices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm finished as a teacher within a couple of years. If a computer can plan and mark and explain long division better than me by 2028, the council will put one adult in a room with fifty kids and a screen each. That adult won't be a slow second-year on a temporary contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd sign every petition and stand on every picket line, because that's the only power people like me have. I'd sit down with Tom and work out whether we could live on his care wages alone. The robots for care work come about three years later, so his job would last longer than mine, which is a strange thing to be grateful for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Like reading a letter you know is bad before you open it. I'd have lost my teaching job before I even got good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come about three years after the thinking AI. Does that gap mean anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, not much, because teaching is mostly talk and planning, and that's the part that goes first. The hands-on part of my job is wiping noses and breaking up fights, and nobody pays a teacher's wage for that. The gap matters more for Tom, because he lifts people and washes them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you couldn't teach, what would you do for money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I genuinely don't know, and that's what scares me. I'd probably go back to the café I worked at during university, if it's still open. That's not a plan, that's just the last place that said yes to me.

say: I'd say nobody **voted for** this, and I'd be at every union meeting and protest.
I'd call it the **biggest decision** a country could make, taken without asking anyone.
think: I expect to be **finished as a teacher** within a couple of years of 2028.
The council would put **one adult** with fifty children and screens, and it wouldn't be me.
do: Sign every **petition** and join every picket line in the first months.
Work out with Tom whether we can live on his **care wages** alone.
Ask the old **café** from university for shifts if teaching goes.
feel: **Sick**, like holding a bad letter before opening it.
Cheated, because she'd lose the job **before getting good** at it.
S2.quote: I'd have lost my teaching job before I even got good at it.
fieldNote: She expects the **thinking parts** of teaching to go on the stated date, leaving little hands-on work worth a wage.
Her only plan is **protest and Tom's wages**; the café is a fallback, not a plan.
The three-year robot gap matters to her only because it protects **Tom's care job** for longer.

steps.text: Join union pickets and protests outside the council offices
Sit down with Tom and budget to live on his care wages
Ask the university café for weekend shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, but louder and with more people, because five years is enough time to organise. I'd be telling people to write to their MP and join the union now, not when the letters come. Five years is a whole election away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives me time to become a proper teacher, which is something. By 2031 I'd have seven years' experience and maybe a permanent contract. But I'd still be in the group that gets cut, because experienced or not, I'm a thinking worker in a thinking job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the branch rep role in the union, which I've been putting off. I'd keep teaching and push hard for a permanent post, because permanent staff get redundancy pay and temporary staff get nothing. And I'd vote in that election like my job depends on it, because it would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a bit of fight in it. Two years felt like a car crash. Five years feels like a storm you can see coming over the hills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd vote like your job depends on it. What would you want a government to actually do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep a qualified teacher in every class by law, full stop. And if the AI firms make fortunes from replacing us, tax them and pay people properly to retrain. I'm not asking for a handout, I'm asking for a share of what we built.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would five years change anything at home with Tom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about a baby in a few years, and I think we'd wait. You don't bring a child into a home where nobody knows if there's a wage in 2031. That's the part that makes me really angry.

say: I'd tell people to **join the union** and write to their MP now, not later.
I'd say five years is a **whole election** away, so there's time to organise.
think: Five years lets me become a **proper teacher**, maybe on a permanent contract.
Experienced or not, I'm still a **thinking worker** in a thinking job.
do: Stand for **branch rep** in the union, a role I've put off.
Push for a **permanent post**, because only permanent staff get redundancy pay.
Vote in the next **election** on this issue above all others.
feel: **Anxious** but with some fight, like watching a storm coming over the hills.
S3.quote: Two years felt like a car crash. Five years feels like a storm you can see coming over the hills.
fieldNote: Extra time turns her fear into **organising**: branch rep, voting, writing to her MP.
She still expects to be **cut by 2031**, so the mood stays high despite the energy.
The scenario reaches into **family plans**; she and Tom would put off having a baby.

steps.text: Stand for union branch rep at Millbrook Primary this year
Vote for a party promising a qualified teacher in every class
Put off trying for a baby with Tom until 2031 looks clearer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to get the rules right, so let's get them right. Write it into law that a child learns from a person. I'd be saying that at the union conference, not just in the staff room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is the difference between losing my job and losing my career halfway through. I'd be 37 in 2036, which is young enough to start again, but old enough to be tired. I'd rather fight for teaching than plan my way out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching and finally get my permanent contract, I hope. I'd stay in the union and push for the law. I'd save what I can, even if it's slow, because ten years of fifty a month is still six thousand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can breathe. It's still the same end point, though, and I don't like that I'd spend ten years waiting for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather fight than plan your way out. What if the fight doesn't work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd retrain into something with people in it, maybe speech therapy for kids, because I'm good with the ones who struggle to talk. But I'd only do that once I'd lost the fight. I'm not giving up my classroom just because a man in a tech company says it's inevitable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the kids in your class be facing by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kai would be eighteen in 2036. He'd be leaving school into a world where the computer can do the thinking jobs. That's what keeps me teaching him to read properly, because a kid who can read can at least argue back.

say: I'd say ten years is **enough time** to get the rules right, so we should.
I'd push at the **union conference** for a law that children learn from a person.
think: Ten years means losing a **career halfway**, not just a first job.
At **37** I could start again, but I'd rather fight for teaching first.
do: Keep teaching and press for a **permanent contract** at Millbrook.
Save **fifty a month**, which adds up to six thousand over ten years.
Look at **speech therapy** training only if the fight for teachers is lost.
feel: **Uneasy** but able to breathe, though she hates waiting ten years for the same end.
S4.quote: I'm not giving up my classroom just because a man in a tech company says it's inevitable.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her **breathe**, but she still expects the job to shrink and money stays thin.
She treats **retraining** as a last resort, which fits her dislike of change.
Her pupils' future, especially **Kai's reading**, is what keeps her in the classroom.

steps.text: Push a no-screens-without-teachers motion at the union conference
Save fifty a month toward a cushion over the decade
Keep teaching Year 3 and chase a permanent contract

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt, because I'd lose the job before I ever got good at it. What would help is a permanent contract now and a law saying a qualified teacher stays in every class. And if it all goes anyway, real money to retrain, not a two-week online course.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who decides. Nobody asked teachers, or Kai's mum, or Tom's care home. A child learning to read needs a person who notices when they're about to cry, and no budget sheet has a line for that.

headlineQuote: A child learning to read needs a person who notices when they're about to cry, and no budget sheet has a line for that.
portrait: Priya is a **second-year** Year 3 teacher in Hadley Bridge, on a one-year contract renewed each July.
She lives above a launderette with **Tom**, a night-shift care worker, with almost nothing saved.
She **never uses AI**, plans by hand, and sees the union as her main source of power.
She is anxious even in AI Plateau, and **alarmed** by fast AGI, which she thinks would end her teaching career.
With more time she **organises and votes** rather than retrains, keeping retraining as a last resort.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she would lose the job before she ever got good at it.
whatWouldHelp: A **permanent contract** now and a law keeping a qualified teacher in every class.
Real **retraining money** if teaching goes, not a two-week online course.
